A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Phantom and retain matching core evaluations. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. All 11 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2, including v2's supplementary materials, are available; v1 has no separately labeled appendix.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original video-generation experiments, identity and subject-consistency scores in Tables 1–2, qualitative comparisons, and a 20-user evaluation in Figure 5.

after.justification: Section 4 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds encoder ablations. The supplementary materials report alignment success rates, training-data distributions and additional qualitative comparisons.

M1.justification: v1 Section 2.2 explicitly describes modifying inputs without changing the DiT structure. v2 instead specifies window attention with dynamic reference-feature injection, shifting and output averaging (Section 3.2, Figure 5). It also introduces an appearance-aware prompt rephraser. These substantially revise the reported procedure beyond retaining the existing VAE/CLIP encoders.

E1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 additionally reports paired-image training data from Subject200k and OmniGen alongside video triplets. The principal evaluation coverage remains single subjects, multiple subjects and facial identity across the same broad categories. Naming Panda70M supplies provenance rather than establishing a new evaluation domain.

E2.justification: Supplementary Figure 9 adds a qualitative comparison against an S2I+I2V pipeline attributed to Dreamina. The original benchmark comparators remain Vidu2.0, Pika2.1, Kling/Keling1.6, Hailuo-ID and ConsisID. Kling replaces the spelling Keling without establishing a different comparator.

E3.justification: The principal benchmark sizes, metrics, frame sampling and user-rating procedure remain unchanged. Added analyses introduce encoder-removal and alignment controls, a success-rate endpoint, and object-distribution measurement using frames at 0.05, 0.5 and 0.95 of video duration. Newly disclosed training budgets do not establish revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v1 lacks controlled ablations. v2 adds VAE/CLIP removal experiments (Table 3, Figure 8) and text-image alignment ablations (Table 4, Figure 12). Its supplement also investigates staged-generation identity loss, copy-paste failures, dataset composition and additional comparator failures, substantially expanding diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: The main evaluation retains three random seeds per text-image pair. Supplementary Section 7 newly specifies that Vidu's shoe-case failure occurred with two different seeds. This is limited additional seed reporting, not evidence of increased benchmark replication. Neither version reports confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original quality/user-study plots retain their values. New Table 3 reports DINO-I of 0.302 without VAE versus 0.523 with both encoders; Table 4 reports 65% success without alignment versus 95% with alignment. New distribution results and qualitative failures expand the evidence. These are added analyses, not demonstrated v1-to-v2 performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 adds mathematical specifications absent from v1: the rectified-flow noise trajectory, velocity target and loss, and separate image/text guidance equation. This is a limited formal addition without theorems or proofs. Equations 1–2 mainly express the already-described feature concatenation mathematically.

C1.justification: v2 adds the priority claim of being first to clearly define S2V and makes dynamic injection and resolving multi-subject confusion explicit central contributions. Its abstract and conclusion also broaden v1's competitiveness and advantage over some commercial solutions into claims of outperforming state-of-the-art commercial solutions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of identity loss in S2I+I2V, encoder-specific artifacts and multi-subject ambiguity. Supplementary Section 8 identifies limitations involving rare subjects, spatial relationships, relative sizes and intricate instructions, attributing them to data and model biases. Conversely, the main results discussion weakens v1's explicit Dynamic Degree warning to an unspecified 'slightly worse' despite retaining the plot.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents data sources, filtering/detection/matching tools, approximately one million cross-pairs and a face-ID pipeline. It supplies 50k plus 20k training iterations, resolution stages, VAE dropout of 0.7, approximately 30,000 A100 GPU-hours, 50-step Euler sampling and guidance weights of 3 and 7.5. These substantially improve implementation transparency without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

R1.justification: The brief positioning in v1 becomes a dedicated three-part related-work section covering video foundations, subject-consistent images and subject-consistent videos. Added works include DreamBooth, PuLID, OmniGen and MovieWeaver. v2 substantially develops its relationship to image-personalization methods and staged S2I+I2V alternatives, alongside the new S2V priority claim.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are substantially rewritten and reorganized. v2 introduces a structured contribution statement, separates related work, adds a training/inference subsection and organizes supplementary material into eight sections. Much of the original benchmark description remains recognizable within this larger narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the data pipeline, revises the architecture diagram and adds attention, ablation, distribution and supplementary pipeline displays. Earlier qualitative panels are selected and combined into Figure 7 or retained in supplementary comparisons. The unchanged v1 Figure 5 plots become v2 Figure 6; their relocation is not new evidence.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of implementation detail and controlled evidence for design choices through Sections 3.2–3.3, Tables 3–4 and the supplementary analyses. Specific limitations also make applicability easier to assess. The new success-rate evaluation remains underspecified, and broader superiority claims plus the weakened Dynamic Degree discussion reduce precision. Nevertheless, the gains in transparency and diagnostic support constitute a substantial overall improvement, independent of the unchanged main benchmark scores.
